query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated, machine-learning-driven computational framework that separately predicts lattice and electronic thermal conductivities in HfNbTaTiZr—by incorporating atomistic disorder, local force-constant fluctuations, and ab initio electronic scattering calculations—will outperform current methods by achieving prediction accuracies within ±10% of experimental values.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr modeled as both defect‐free bulk crystals and samples containing ~1 wt.% oxygen impurities.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a first‐principles informed machine-learning interatomic potential that independently quantifies phonon scattering (through local disorder and mass fluctuation analysis) and electronic scattering (via ab initio evaluation of electronic structure).
generation.conditions: The approach is applied across a broad temperature range: below 200 K (where lattice and electronic contributions are observed to be comparable) and from 300 to 1200 K (matching conditions in oxygen-containing samples with reported total conductivities between 10–17 W/(K·m)).
generation.structural_mediator: Disorder-induced variations in local force constants and mass distribution mediate the phonon scattering, while detailed electronic structure parameters provide a basis for evaluating electronic scattering processes.
generation.mechanism: The method bypasses oversimplified Debye temperature approximations by using a machine-learning potential to capture atomic-scale variations and disorder effects, decoupling the traditional conflation of lattice and electronic transport channels and thereby enabling independent and accurate predictions of each contribution.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will accurately decompose the overall thermal conductivity into its lattice and electronic components, achieving prediction accuracies within ±10% of experimental measurements. Below 200 K, the predictions will show nearly equal contributions from each channel; at higher temperatures, the summed conductivity will fall within the 10–17 W/(K·m) range observed in oxygen-containing samples.
generation.baseline: Earlier models based on DFT-derived elastic properties and Debye temperature–dependent analytical estimates, which assume defect‐free crystals and conflate phonon and electron transport contributions.
generation.boundary: The predictive improvement holds for HfNbTaTiZr and similar refractory high-entropy alloys under the studied temperature ranges and impurity levels (up to ~1 wt.% oxygen). It might be limited if additional unaccounted scattering mechanisms become dominant or for substantially different compositions.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty regarding the precise improvement magnitude due to the complex interplay of impurity effects and potential additional scattering processes not fully captured in the training data.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct separate experiments to measure lattice thermal conductivity via low-temperature phonon spectroscopy and to evaluate electronic transport using electrical conductivity measurements. Test specimens should include both pure and ~1 wt.% oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr samples over the temperature range below 200 K and between 300–1200 K.
measurements: Total thermal conductivity between 300 K and 1200 K in oxygen-containing specimens
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the independently measured lattice or electronic conductivities deviate by more than ±10% from the model’s predictions, or if the summed predictions do not match the experimentally observed total conductivity within that margin over the specified temperature range, then the hypothesis is falsified.

decision.trend: Earlier work on thermal transport in high‐entropy alloys proceeded in two largely separate directions. Initial studies using DFT-derived elastic properties and quasi-analytical methods (relying on parameters like the Debye temperature) assumed defect‐free crystals and hence produced combined estimates of lattice and electronic conductivities that did not capture local atomic-scale disorder. Later, studies such as the scaling-law work (PMC10983832) began to quantify the influence of lattice distortion and chemical disorder on phonon dynamics – establishing that static and dynamic lattice distortions can be unified via an effective temperature – while separate studies (PMC11136967) addressed conduction using the cocktail effect and effective medium models for the electronic part. Each work improved understanding of individual scattering mechanisms yet failed to integrate these effects to yield independently predictable components across the full temperature range.
decision.unsolved: The major unresolved issue is to develop a single predictive framework that does not conflate lattice and electronic contributions but instead decouples them in refractory HEAs like HfNbTaTiZr. Existing models either oversimplify by using ideal-crystal assumptions or mix phonon and electron transport parameters, failing to reflect the complexity seen in experiments (such as comparable contributions below 200 K and impurity effects at high temperatures).
decision.lever: Develop an integrated, first‐principles informed, machine‐learning interatomic potential that separately treats phonon scattering (by capturing local force-constant fluctuations and mass disorder) and electronic scattering (via ab initio evaluation of electronic structure and scattering rates).
decision.why: This approach follows naturally from the trend: earlier methods either focused on lattice dynamics or electronic conduction but did not couple the two. By leveraging machine learning to parameterize both the disorder-induced force-constant variations (as shown by the scaling law in PMC10983832) and refined electronic scattering mechanisms (as in PMC11136967), the new approach can predict each transport channel separately. It is expected to outperform previous strategies by reducing prediction error (targeting accuracies within ±10% of experimental values) and by being applicable across a broad temperature range – below 200 K for samples with nearly equal lattice and electronic conduction and from 300 to 1200 K in real, impurity-containing alloys. Decisive falsification would occur if low-temperature measurements (via phonon spectroscopy) or high-temperature total conductivity measurements (in ~1 wt.% oxygen samples) deviate significantly from the independently predicted values.
